lessons.title: ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ñān pōkunnu) — I go, and I am going
lessons.gloss: I go — and also I am going; one Malayalam form answers two different English questions

segments.text: Say I go. Then say it for you and for they — and notice that the verb did not move.
You were told that Malayalam's present tense is one word for everybody. Here is the part that was not said:
It is also one word for two English tenses.

utterances: ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു, ñān pōkunnu, I go.
ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു, ñān pōkunnu, I am going.

segments.text: Those are the same Malayalam sentence, written twice. English asks you to choose — I go to work against I am going to work — and the choice does not exist here. There is nothing to get right.

English is the unusual one. Most languages do not split the present into a habitual and an ongoing form, and Malayalam does not. -ുന്നു covers what you do every day and what you are doing at this moment, and a listener takes whichever the situation offers.
This is not a gap in Malayalam. When it matters which you mean, the language says so with another word rather than another verb form — which is the next lesson.

segments.instruction: ñān pōkunnu — and mean I go
ñān pōkunnu again — and mean I am going
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ñān pōkunnu* again — and mean *I am going*]

segments.instruction: the same for to come — ñān varunnu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same for *to come* — *ñān varunnu*]

segments.instruction: what English makes you choose that Malayalam does not
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what English makes you choose that Malayalam does not]

segments.text: How do you say I go? (ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ñān pōkunnu).) How do you say I am going? (The same — ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ñān pōkunnu).) Which language is doing the extra work here? (English — it splits a present that Malayalam keeps whole.)

lessons.title: ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu) — right now, I am going
lessons.gloss: right now I am going — the word that pins the present to this moment, and you have owned it for a long while

segments.text: Say I am going. Then say the word for now.
The last lesson left one thing open: if ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ñān pōkunnu) can mean either, how do you say you mean this moment?
You put the moment in front of it.
ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു. — ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu — "Right now I am going."
The verb did not change. Not one letter of it. What changed is that a word naming the moment is standing at the front, and it is a word you have owned for a long while.

That front position is not new either. ഇന്ന് has stood there, and നാളെ, and a named day, and an hour with an ending on it. ഇപ്പോൾ is the same slot doing the narrowest version of its job: not today, not this Monday — now.
This is how Malayalam answers a question English answers with the verb. English changes go into am going. Malayalam leaves the verb alone and adds a word — and a word is easier than a form.

segments.instruction: ñān pōkunnu, then ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu
the same with to come — ippōḷ ñān varunnu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same with *to come* — *ippōḷ ñān varunnu*]

segments.instruction: which part of the sentence changed, and which did not
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which part of the sentence changed, and which did not]

segments.text: How do you say right now I am going? (ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu).) What happened to the verb? (Nothing — it is unchanged.) Where did ഇപ്പോൾ go? (At the front, in the slot that says when.)

lessons.title: ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ വരുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān varunnu) — and there is no word for am
lessons.gloss: right now I am coming — and there is no word here for "am", which is the mistake this lesson exists to stop

segments.text: Say to come. Then say right now I am going.
The rule is general, so take a second verb through it:
ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ വരുന്നു. — ippōḷ ñān varunnu — "Right now I am coming."
You built that yourself. varuka has been yours for a long time, and the -ുന്നു ending is the one you were told makes the whole present tense. Nobody had to give you varunnu as a word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the word you must not reach for

segments.text: English says I am going, in two words. When you go looking for the Malayalam word to put where am is, you will find ആണ് — because ആണ് is the word you were given for is and am, in your very first week.
Do not put it here.

utterances: ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ വരുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān varunnu), right — one verb, nothing added.
ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ ആണ് വരുന്നു, not a Malayalam sentence.

segments.text: ആണ് joins a thing to what it is — a name, a description. It is not a helper that props up another verb, because Malayalam has no such helpers. The whole of am going lives inside വരുന്നു.

segments.instruction: ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu, then the coming one again
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu*, then the coming one again]

segments.instruction: where English puts am, and what Malayalam puts there instead
segments.source: [YOU SAY: where English puts *am*, and what Malayalam puts there instead]

segments.text: Right now I am coming? (ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ വരുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān varunnu).) How many words carry am coming? (One — വരുന്നു.) Does ആണ് belong in that sentence? (No — it joins a thing to what it is; it does not help another verb.)

lessons.title: എപ്പോൾ — ഇപ്പോൾ (eppōḷ — ippōḷ) — asked and answered
lessons.gloss: when? — right now; a question you own and an answer you own, one letter apart

segments.text: Say when? Then say now. Say them one after the other and listen to how little separates them.
You own both halves of an exchange and have never put them together:
One vowel apart, and they are question and answer. The ഇ- points at something; the എ- asks about it. That single vowel is carrying the whole difference between pointing and asking.
— നീ എപ്പോൾ വരുന്നു? — nī eppōḷ varunnu? — "When are you coming?" — ഞാൻ ഇപ്പോൾ വരുന്നു. — ñān ippōḷ varunnu. — "I am coming right now."

Look at what did not change. Two different people are speaking about two different subjects, and വരുന്നു is identical in both lines. The verb carried the asking and the answering without moving a letter.
That is what this chapter has been about: Malayalam puts the work in a word at the front, and leaves the verb alone. English puts the work in the verb.

segments.instruction: nī eppōḷ varunnu?, then ñān ippōḷ varunnu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *nī eppōḷ varunnu?*, then *ñān ippōḷ varunnu*]

segments.instruction: which single vowel carries the difference between asking and pointing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which single vowel carries the difference between asking and pointing]

segments.text: When? (എപ്പോൾ.) Now? (ഇപ്പോൾ.) Which vowel asks and which one points? (എ- asks, ഇ- points.) How much of the verb changed between question and answer? (None of it.)

lessons.title: (I go, I am going, right now) (ippōḷ enna ōrmma) — from cold
lessons.headword: (I go, I am going, right now)
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the one present form, the word that pins it to this moment, and the helper Malayalam does not have

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say I go, then I am going, then right now I am going.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one form, and a word in front of it

utterances: ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു, ñān pōkunnu, I go and I am going.
ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു, ippōḷ ñān pōkunnu, right now I am going.

segments.text: The verb is the same in both rows. That is the whole chapter in one column. Where English changes go to am going and then adds right now, Malayalam never touches the verb at all — it puts a word in the slot at the front, the same slot that has held today, tomorrow, a named day and a named hour.

Not one word in this chapter was new. The verb ending was named for you long ago; ഇപ്പോൾ and എപ്പോൾ have both been yours for chapters. What you did not have was permission to use one form for two English tenses, and the warning that goes with it.

That warning is worth keeping. English's am has no home in ഇപ്പോൾ ഞാൻ വരുന്നു (ippōḷ ñān varunnu). ആണ് exists, and it joins a thing to what it is — it is not a helper for another verb, because Malayalam has none.

segments.instruction: ñān pōkunnu, meaning each of the two English sentences in turn
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ñān pōkunnu*, meaning each of the two English sentences in turn]

segments.text: Two English sentences, one Malayalam one — which? (I go and I am going, both ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (ñān pōkunnu).) How do you pin it to this moment? (ഇപ്പോൾ, at the front.) Where does am go? (Nowhere — it is inside the verb.)
